benchmark_name: Day 06 Data Ingestion Engineering Benchmark - IETF OAuth 2.0 & JWT Security Corpus
split_policy: Stratified split frozen prior to running retrieval experiments: 15 dev questions (q01-q15) and 5 test questions (q16-q20) balanced across the 4 RFC documents (rfc8693, rfc8725, rfc9068, rfc9126) and 4 question types (direct, paraphrase, conditional, metadata_filter). Includes 5 metadata_filter questions (3 in dev, 2 in test) using only pre-retrieval context metadata (year, category) without leaking gold_source_id or answers.
selection_criteria: Primary: highest Dev Evidence Hit@3; Secondary: highest Dev Hit@1 and manual Grounding/Coherence score; Tertiary: lowest chunk count and ingestion time.

questions.question: In OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, what does the outermost 'act' claim represent when a chain of delegation is expressed by nesting 'act' claims?
questions.expected_answer: The outermost 'act' claim represents the current actor, while nested 'act' claims represent prior actors (with the least recent actor being the most deeply nested).
questions.evidence_quote:
A chain of delegation can be expressed by nesting one act claim within another. The outermost
act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors. The least
recent actor is the most deeply nested.

questions.question: How do 'delegation' and 'impersonation' differ when resource server A calls backend service C on behalf of user B?
questions.expected_answer: In delegation, A uses its own credentials to access C with an annotation that A is acting on behalf of B; in impersonation, A is granted a limited access credential to C that continues to identify B as the authorized entity.
questions.evidence_quote:
it may be desirable for A to use its own
credentials to access C along with an annotation of some form that A is acting on behalf of B
("delegation") or for A to be granted a limited access credential to C but that continues to identify
B as the authorized entity ("impersonation").

questions.question: How can an attacker exploit elliptic curve key agreement ('ECDH-ES') when a JOSE library fails to validate curve point inputs?
questions.expected_answer: By sending JWEs that use invalid curve points and observing the cleartext outputs resulting from decryption, the attacker can recover the recipient's private key.
questions.evidence_quote:
An
attacker that is able to send JWEs of its choosing that use invalid curve points and observe the
cleartext outputs resulting from decryption with the invalid curve points can use this
vulnerability to recover the recipient's private key.

questions.question: Why should human-memorizable passwords not be directly used as the key to a keyed-MAC algorithm like HS256 in JWTs, and what should they be used for instead?
questions.expected_answer: Human-memorizable passwords MUST NOT be directly used as the key to a keyed-MAC algorithm such as HS256; passwords should only be used to perform key encryption rather than content encryption.
questions.evidence_quote:
human-memorizable Section 8.8 of [ RFC7518 ] MUST
passwords be directly used as the key to a keyed-MAC algorithm such as "HS256". MUST NOT
Moreover, passwords should only be used to perform key encryption, rather than content
encryption

questions.question: When applying explicit typing to a Nested JWT, where must the 'typ' Header Parameter containing the explicit type value be present?
questions.expected_answer: It MUST be present in the inner JWT of the Nested JWT (whose payload is the JWT Claims Set), and in some cases may also be present in the outer JWT.
questions.evidence_quote:
When applying explicit typing to a Nested JWT, the "typ" Header Parameter containing the
explicit type value be present in the inner JWT of the Nested JWT (the JWT whose payload MUST
is the JWT Claims Set).

questions.question: According to the 2020 Best Current Practice specification, under what condition can the 'none' algorithm be acceptable for a JWT?
questions.expected_answer: When the JWT is cryptographically protected end-to-end by another transport layer, such as TLS using cryptographically current algorithms, and only when explicitly requested by the caller.
questions.evidence_quote:
That said, if a JWT is cryptographically protected end-to-end by a transport layer, such as TLS
using cryptographically current algorithms, there may be no need to apply another layer of
cryptographic protections to the JWT. In such cases, the use of the "none" algorithm can be
perfectly acceptable.

questions.question: In the JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens, how does the expected value of the 'sub' claim differ between grants involving a resource owner versus the client credentials grant?
questions.expected_answer: When a resource owner is involved (e.g., authorization code grant), 'sub' SHOULD correspond to the subject identifier of the resource owner; when no resource owner is involved (e.g., client credentials grant), 'sub' SHOULD correspond to an identifier the authorization server uses to indicate the client application.
questions.evidence_quote:
In cases of access tokens obtained REQUIRED Section 4.1.2 of [ RFC7519 ]
through grants where a resource owner is involved, such as the authorization code grant, the
value of "sub" correspond to the subject identifier of the resource owner. In cases of SHOULD
access tokens obtained through grants where no resource owner is involved, such as the client
credentials grant, the value of "sub" correspond to an identifier the authorization SHOULD
server uses to indicate the client application.

questions.question: Why are OAuth 2.0 clients prohibited from inspecting the contents of a JWT access token?
questions.expected_answer: Because the authorization server and resource server might decide to change the token format at any time (such as switching to opaque tokens), which would break any client logic relying on reading the token's content.
questions.evidence_quote:
The client inspect the content of the access token: the authorization server and the MUST NOT
resource server might decide to change the token format at any time (for example, by switching
from this profile to opaque tokens); hence, any logic in the client relying on the ability to read the
access token content would break without recourse.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'may_act' claim in a JWT subject token during an OAuth 2.0 token exchange request?
questions.expected_answer: The 'may_act' claim states that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party, allowing the authorization server to determine whether the client or actor_token party is eligible for the requested delegation or impersonation.
questions.evidence_quote:
The may_act claim makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act
on behalf of another party. The claim might be used, for example, when a subject_token is
presented to the token endpoint in a token exchange request and may_act claim in the subject
token can be used by the authorization server to determine whether the client (or party
identified in the actor_token ) is authorized to engage in the requested delegation or
impersonation.

questions.question: According to the 2020 Best Current Practice specification, how can blindly following a 'jku' or 'x5u' header parameter in a JWT be exploited, and how should applications defend against it?
questions.expected_answer: It can result in server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks; applications SHOULD protect against this by matching the URL against a whitelist of allowed locations and ensuring no cookies are sent in the GET request.
questions.evidence_quote:
Similarly, blindly following a "jku" (JWK set URL) or "x5u" (X.509 URL) header, which may
contain an arbitrary URL, could result in server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks. Applications
protect against such attacks, e.g., by matching the URL to a whitelist of allowed locations SHOULD
and ensuring no cookies are sent in the GET request.

questions.question: Under the 2021 Standards Track specification, what signing algorithm policy applies to the 'none' algorithm and what media type is used in the 'typ' header parameter for JWT access tokens?
questions.expected_answer: JWT access tokens MUST be signed (with RS256 required to be supported), MUST NOT use 'none' as the signing algorithm, and MUST include the 'application/at+jwt' media type (recommended as 'at+jwt') in the 'typ' header parameter.
questions.evidence_quote:
JWT access tokens use MUST NOT
"none" as the signing algorithm. See Section 4 for more details.

Authorization servers and resource servers conforming to this specification include RS256 MUST
(as defined in ) among their supported signature algorithms. [ RFC7518 ]

This specification registers the "application/at+jwt" media type, which can be used to indicate that
the content is a JWT access token.

questions.expected_answer: The client MUST only use a 'request_uri' value once because parts of the authorization request content (such as the 'code_challenge' parameter value) are unique to a particular authorization request.
questions.evidence_quote:
Since parts of the authorization request content, e.g., the code_challenge parameter value, are
unique to a particular authorization request, the client only use a request_uri value once. MUST

questions.question: In Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR), what is the default value of the 'require_pushed_authorization_requests' metadata parameter if omitted, and does a client need 'request_uri_parameter_supported' to use a PAR request_uri?
questions.expected_answer: If omitted, the default value of 'require_pushed_authorization_requests' is false; a 'request_uri' obtained from the PAR endpoint is usable at the authorization endpoint regardless of other metadata such as 'request_uri_parameter_supported' or 'require_request_uri_registration'.
questions.evidence_quote:
require_pushed_authorization_requests
Boolean parameter indicating whether the authorization server accepts authorization request
data only via PAR. If omitted, the default value is false .

Note that the presence of pushed_authorization_request_endpoint is sufficient for a client to
determine that it may use the PAR flow. A request_uri value obtained from the PAR endpoint is
usable at the authorization endpoint regardless of other authorization server metadata such as
request_uri_parameter_supported or require_request_uri_registration
